name: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
description: SNAP gives eligible low-income households a monthly benefit on an EBT card (the Lone Star Card in Texas) to buy groceries. Households must meet income and resource limits and apply in the state where they live. In Texas, households with gross monthly income up to 165% of the federal poverty level can qualify through categorical eligibility; the federal baseline is 130% gross and 100% net. Households with an elderly or disabled member only have to meet the net income test. Federal resource limits are $3,000, or $4,750 if a member is 60 or older or disabled, though many states relax them. Immigration rules and work rules apply, and USDA notes they changed under 2025 legislation. For October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027, the maximum monthly benefit is $306 for one person and $1,023 for four. Applications are normally decided within 30 days, and some households in urgent need can get benefits within 7 days.
documents_needed: Proof of citizenship or immigration status
source: USDA Food and Nutrition Administration; Texas Health and Human Services

name: Medicaid
description: Medicaid is a joint federal and state program that provides free or low-cost health coverage to some low-income people, including families and children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with disabilities. Income limits differ by group. The Medicaid.gov Texas profile, with a table dated December 1, 2023, lists 198% of the federal poverty level for children ages 0 to 1 and for pregnant women, 144% for ages 1 to 5, 133% for ages 6 to 18, and 12% for parents and caretakers, with no expansion to other adults; separate CHIP is 201%. The figure recorded here is the highest Medicaid band. Texas runs separate programs for children, pregnant women, parents and caretakers, and older adults and people with disabilities. HealthCare.gov says a recent law change limits full Medicaid and CHIP to certain immigration statuses. States must decide most applications within 45 days, or 90 days when based on disability. The monthly value shown is an estimate of government spending, not cash you receive: Medicaid benefit spending per Texas enrollee in fiscal year 2023, divided by 12.
documents_needed: Proof of citizenship or immigration status
Medical bills from the past three months
source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; Texas Health and Human Services

name: Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC)
description: WIC provides healthy foods, nutrition counseling, breastfeeding support, and health referrals for pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women, infants, and children up to age 5. Applicants must live in the state where they apply, be found at nutritional risk through a free health screening, and have household income at or below 185% of the federal poverty level, unless they or their children already get Medicaid, SNAP, or TANF, which can meet the income test. Texas uses the federal maximum: from July 2026 through June 2027 that is $2,461 a month for one person and $5,088 for a household of four. U.S. citizenship is not required. Texas applicants start online or by phone with a local WIC office and then attend an appointment. If a WIC office is full, a priority system decides who is served first. Pregnant women stay on WIC until the end of pregnancy, and infants and children until they turn 5.
documents_needed: Proof of SNAP, Medicaid, or TANF participation
source: USDA Food and Nutrition Administration; Texas Health and Human Services

name: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
description: LIHEAP is a federal program that helps low-income households with home energy costs, including heating and cooling bills, energy crises, weatherization, and minor energy-related repairs. In Texas it runs as the Comprehensive Energy Assistance Program (CEAP) through the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, which funds local providers in all 254 counties and does not take applications from individuals. Texas calculates CEAP eligibility at 150% of the federal poverty income guidelines; for 2026 that is $23,940 a year for a one-person household and $49,500 for a household of four. Providers verify that household members are U.S. citizens or qualified non-citizens. Crisis help is provided within 48 hours for extreme weather or disasters and within 18 hours for life-threatening situations. Providers can run out of funds. LIHEAP does not charge a fee. The monthly value shown is an estimate: the lower of Texas's fiscal year 2023 average yearly household benefits ($1,751 cooling, $2,750 heating), spread over 12 months. Actual help is seasonal or one-time.
documents_needed: Income documents for all adult household members
Proof of citizenship or qualified immigration status
source: ACF Office of Community Services; Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs

name: Medicare Part D Extra Help (Low-Income Subsidy)
description: Extra Help is a Medicare program that lowers Medicare drug plan (Part D) premiums, deductibles, and copays for people with limited income and resources. To qualify you generally need Medicare Part A or Part B, must live in one of the 50 states or the District of Columbia, and must have income below 150% of the federal poverty level. In 2026 Medicare lists the limits as $23,940 of income for an individual and $32,460 for a married couple, with resource limits of $18,090 and $36,100. You get Extra Help automatically if you have full Medicaid, help from a Medicare Savings Program, or SSI. Others can apply through the Social Security Administration online or by phone. To join a Medicare drug plan you must be a U.S. citizen or have a qualifying immigration status. Extra Help is not available in the U.S. territories. The monthly value shown is an estimate: SSA's stated yearly worth of Extra Help, about $5,700, divided by 12. It is an average, not your own amount.
documents_needed: Pension, Veterans' benefits, annuity, and Railroad Retirement Board statements
source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; Social Security Administration

name: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)
description: SSDI, which the Social Security Administration also calls Disability, pays a monthly benefit and, later, Medicare to people who cannot work because of a medical condition. You need a disability or blindness that affects your ability to work for a year or more or will result in death, and enough work history under Social Security. Generally that means working at least 5 of the last 10 years, with exceptions for people under 24. In 2026, you generally cannot qualify if you earn more than $1,690 a month ($2,830 if blind). There is usually a five-month waiting period before payments start, and Medicare begins 2 years after entitlement. The average disabled-worker benefit was $1,635.90 a month in August 2026, but your own amount depends on your earnings record. SSA says an initial decision generally takes 6 to 8 months. You must be a U.S. citizen or a lawfully present noncitizen. Disability benefits convert to retirement benefits at full retirement age. The 240 day processing figure is an estimate that converts 8 months at 30 days each.
documents_needed: Doctor, hospital, and clinic names and phone numbers
Earnings history and recent employer details
Bank routing and account number for direct deposit
Workers' compensation claim details, if any

name: Head Start
description: Head Start gives free early learning, health and family support services to young children from low-income families and helps prepare them for school. Head Start Preschool programs mainly serve 3- and 4-year-old children. Your family may qualify if its income is at or below the federal poverty level, and programs may enroll some children from families with higher incomes if they meet other requirements. A family may also qualify if it is experiencing homelessness, has children in foster care, or is receiving TANF or SSI. To apply, contact the program closest to where you live. The program provides the forms and tells you which documents you should bring.
source: U.S. Administration for Children and Families

name: Early Head Start
description: Early Head Start serves infants and toddlers under the age of 3, and pregnant women, from low-income families with child development and family support services. Your family may qualify if its income is at or below the federal poverty level, and programs may enroll some children from families with higher incomes if they meet other requirements. A family may also qualify if it is experiencing homelessness, has children in foster care, or is receiving TANF or SSI. To apply, contact the program closest to where you live. The local program provides the required forms, answers your questions and tells you what documents you should bring.
source: U.S. Administration for Children and Families

name: School Breakfast Program
description: The School Breakfast Program gives children breakfast at school at a free or reduced price. Any child at a participating school may buy a breakfast. Children from families with incomes at or below 130% of the federal poverty level get free breakfasts, and children from families with incomes between 130% and 185% get reduced-price breakfasts. Children from families over 185% of poverty pay full price, though their meals are still subsidized to some extent. You may apply for school meals any time during the school year by submitting an application directly to your school or district.

name: Summer Meals for Kids (Summer Food Service Program)
description: Through the Summer Food Service Program, kids aged 18 and under can get free meals and snacks during the summer at schools, parks and other neighborhood locations in eligible areas. Open sites operate in low-income areas where at least half of the children come from families with incomes at or below 185% of the federal poverty level, and meals are served free to any child at an open site, so the household's own income is not tested. Families can use the Summer Meals for Kids Site Finder to find directions to nearby meal sites, their hours and contact information. In rural areas, sponsors can operate meal pick-up sites or offer home meal delivery.

name: Medicare (Parts A and B)
description: Medicare is the federal health insurance program for people age 65 or older. You sign up for Medicare Part A and Part B through Social Security, which can withhold any premiums from your benefit payments. If you are under age 65, you may be eligible if you have permanent kidney failure or if you receive Social Security Disability benefits. Supplemental Security Income alone does not qualify you for Medicare, so you must meet one of the other requirements. If you are 65 or older you can enroll online for Parts A and B, or Part A only, and you can delay Part B if you are already covered through an employer group health plan.

name: Social Security Retirement Benefits
description: Social Security retirement benefits are monthly payments you can typically start getting at age 62 if you have worked and paid Social Security taxes for 10 years or more. In most cases you can apply while you are still working. The amount depends on your own work record, and Social Security's retirement planning tools can help you estimate your benefit amount and decide when to apply. This is not a poverty-based program: it rests on your age and your work history rather than your household income.

name: Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
description: Supplemental Security Income pays monthly benefits to people with disabilities and older adults who have little or no income or resources. Adults and children might be eligible if they have little or no income, little or no resources, and a disability, blindness, or are age 65 or older. Your monthly payment depends on your income, living situation, things you own, and other factors. The federal payment rate for one person is about $994 a month in 2026, so the poverty percent and the monthly value shown are estimates based on that rate. Social Security's website explains how to apply.

name: Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
description: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a federal tax credit for people who work and have lower incomes. How much you can claim depends on how many qualifying children you have and your income. For tax year 2025 the maximum credit is $649 with no qualifying children, $4,328 with one, $7,152 with two and $8,046 with three or more. The income limit for a single filer ranges from $19,104 with no children to $61,555 with three or more, and investment income must be $11,950 or less. The poverty percent shown is an estimate for a single parent with one child, the highest of the household types.

name: Child Tax Credit
description: The Child Tax Credit is worth up to $2,200 per qualifying child. For the 2025 tax year a qualifying child must be under 17 at the end of the year and be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national or U.S. resident alien. If you have little or no federal income tax, you may qualify for the Additional Child Tax Credit, up to $1,700 per qualifying child depending on your income, and you must have earned income of at least $2,500 for it. You qualify for the full credit if your income is not more than $200,000 ($400,000 on a joint return). The monthly value is an estimate of the maximum credit for one child spread over a year.

name: Free Tax Help (VITA and TCE)
description: Volunteer Income Tax Assistance gives free tax return help to people who need assistance preparing their own tax returns. It serves people who generally make about $70,244 or less, people with disabilities and limited English-speaking taxpayers. The related Tax Counseling for the Elderly program offers free tax help, particularly for people who are 60 years of age and older, and specializes in questions about pensions and retirement-related issues. The IRS manages the programs, and the sites are operated by IRS partners. The poverty percent shown is an estimate for a one-person household, the highest of the household sizes.

name: Community Health Centers (Sliding Fee Discounts)
description: Community health centers funded through the federal Health Center Program offer primary care with a sliding fee discount program based on family size and income. HRSA's example schedule uses discount classes of 101% to 125%, 126% to 150%, 151% to 175% and 176% to 200% of the federal poverty guideline, with partial discounts for people above the poverty line and up to 200%. Eligibility for the discount rests only on family size and income. You can use HRSA's Find a Health Center tool to locate a center near you and ask about its sliding fee scale.

name: Job Corps
description: Job Corps is a free career training program for low-income young people ages 16 to 24. You may be eligible if you are a U.S. citizen, legal U.S. resident, resident of a U.S. territory or authorized to work in the United States, and you are interested in career training, earning a high school diploma or equivalent, and preparing for work or further education. In some cases the upper age limit can be waived for a person with a disability. An Admissions Representative reviews each application after you submit it. You may not be eligible if you use drugs illegally under federal law, show behavior that could prevent you or others from succeeding, or have certain criminal convictions or need court supervision.

name: Title X Family Planning Services
description: Title X is the federal family planning program. Its clinics provide services to any person who wants them, with priority given to people from low-income families. No charge is made for services to a person from a low-income family, except to the extent that a third party, including a government agency, is authorized or legally obligated to pay. Charges for people whose income exceeds 250% of the federal poverty level follow a schedule of fees, and people in between pay on a sliding scale based on ability to pay. Clinics that also receive health center funding may use a 101% to 200% schedule for general care and a 101% to 250% schedule for Title X-only family planning.

name: Free Civil Legal Aid (Legal Services Corporation)
description: Legal Services Corporation funds nonprofit organizations that provide free civil legal aid to low-income Americans. LSC-funded programs can serve households whose net income does not exceed 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines issued each year by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, subject to the local program's own policies. Programs may adopt policies to find some applicants eligible with incomes between 125% and 200% of the guidelines when other factors affect their ability to afford legal assistance. Enter an address or city in LSC's search tool to find the legal aid organization near you.

name: Ticket to Work
description: Social Security's Ticket to Work Program supports career development for people ages 18 through 64 who receive Social Security disability benefits (SSDI or SSI) and want to work. It is free and voluntary. If you qualify, you work with service providers, such as Employment Networks or your State Vocational Rehabilitation agency, to get supports like career counseling, vocational rehabilitation, job placement and training. The service provider you choose becomes part of your employment team and helps you find and keep a job.

name: Work Incentives Planning and Assistance (WIPA)
description: Work Incentives Planning and Assistance projects are organizations funded by Social Security to provide free benefits counseling to all Social Security beneficiaries, regardless of whether they are participating in the Ticket to Work program. The projects are staffed by Community Work Incentive Coordinators, who give individualized, in-depth counseling about working, earning more money and how working may affect your Social Security, health care and other public benefits. A counselor can help you understand specific work incentives, understand the services of your State Vocational Rehabilitation agency or an Employment Network, and decide whether the Ticket program is right for you.
